_strings.@@5877cb897948: Renter's Refund (Renter's Property Tax Refund / circuit-breaker) — A North Dakota renter who is age 65 or older OR has a permanent and total disability, whose income (including spouse and dependents) does not exceed $70,000. Rent must be for the renter's place of residence or a mobile home lot (heat, water, lights, telephone, and furniture costs do not count as rent). For a married couple living together, only one spouse may apply. There is no asset limitation for renters.

Qualifies only if joint ND taxable income (Form ND-1 line 18) exceeds $74,862 AND the lower-earning spouse's qualified income exceeds $43,980. Designed to offset the higher tax that two-earner couples pay versus filing as singles.
_strings.@@9b28c6d02d20: Schedule ND-1NR (Tax Calculation for Nonresidents and Part-Year Residents), filed with Form ND-1. (Nonresidents and part-year residents file Form ND-1 plus Schedule ND-1NR; they cannot use Form ND-EZ.)
_strings.@@a3e2851aad33: Treaty conformity — ND does NOT conform to federal tax treaties: income exempt from federal tax under a treaty is STILL taxable by ND. Do not carry a federal treaty exclusion onto the state return. (This is about TREATY conformity only — a state's Internal Revenue Code conformity date and its deduction/credit conformity are separate questions; see any law-change lines below.) State note: ND does NOT conform — it re-taxes federally treaty-exempt income. Although the ND-1 resident return starts from federal taxable income (Form 1040/1040-SR line 15, ND-1 line 1b), the 2023 ND-1 Individual Income Tax Booklet (p.5) states: "Except where an income tax treaty between the United States and a foreign country specifically exempts income from taxation by a U.S. state, income tax treaties between the U.S. and foreign countries do not apply for North Dakota income tax purposes. Therefore, you may have to pay North Dakota income tax on gross income from North Dakota sources even though the income is exempt from U.S. income tax because of a treaty." The mechanism is in the Guideline: Income Taxation of Nonresident Aliens — the taxpayer must complete a Pro Forma U.S. Form 1040NR but "you must disregard any instruction to the U.S. income tax return that refers to the treaty," then carry that pro-forma 1040NR line 15 (with treaty income NOT excluded) to ND-1 line 1b. So treaty-exempt income that drops out of the actual federal return is effectively added back (rebuilt) before flowing into ND income. This is the same non-conforming posture as CA/CT/MD/MS. The treaty pass-through applies ONLY where a treaty article specifically extends the exemption to the 50 U.S. states.
_strings.@@a90893f07aef: Homestead Property Tax Credit — A North Dakota homeowner who is age 65 or older OR has a permanent and total disability (no age requirement for disability), who lives in and owns the property, and whose income (including spouse and dependents) does not exceed $70,000. For a married couple living together, only one spouse may apply. There is no asset limitation for homeowners. Disability applicants must include a physician's certificate.

state_tax.work_common_tail: . Tax line: Form ND-1 (2023), page 2, line 20: "Tax - If full-year resident, enter tax on amount on line 19 from Tax Table in instructions. If full-year nonresident or part-year resident, enter tax from Schedule ND-1NR, line 23. All filers: If you have farm income or sold a research credit, see instructions." This op computes the state's rate-schedule tax line ONLY — county/city add-on taxes, state credits, and any amounts outside the rate schedule are NOT modeled. Pack notes: Base guidance: Supply federal taxable income — Form 1040/1040-SR line 15, which is entered on Form ND-1 line 1b. If any North Dakota additions (ND-1 lines 2-4a) or subtractions (lines 5-17, e.g. U.S.-obligation interest, net long-term capital gain exclusion, qualified dividend exclusion, Social Security exclusion) apply, supply Form ND-1 line 19 (North Dakota taxable income, carried from line 18 = line 1b + additions - subtractions, floored at 0) instead. The brackets apply directly to that figure with nothing further subtracted: North Dakota has no state standard deduction and no personal/dependent exemptions — the federal standard/itemized deduction is already embedded in federal taxable income. Nonresident-alien edge case: ND does not conform to federal treaty exemptions; an NRA must build a Pro Forma 1040NR disregarding treaty provisions and use its line 15 as ND-1 line 1b. 2023 rate reform (final schedule used for the 2023 filing season): per the 2023 booklet p.2, 'Effective beginning with tax year 2023, the existing five-bracket system for individuals, estates, and trusts was replaced with a three-bracket system. Notably, there is now a 0% bracket and the highest rate was reduced from 2.9% to 2.5%.' The shipped 0%/1.95%/2.5% schedules are the ones printed in the final 2023 booklet (p.28). Tax Table mandate below $100,000: booklet p.15 'Line 20 - Tax' instructs full-year residents to 'use the Tax Table on page 20 to calculate your tax'; the 2023 Tax Table (pp.20-27, $50 income bands) covers ND taxable income under $100,000 and itself says 'If $100,000 or over — use the Tax Rate Schedules.' Bracket math may differ from the table by about a dollar within a band (table values appear to be the schedule evaluated at the band midpoint — the booklet's own example, MFJ $90,375, gives $305, which equals the bracket math rounded); the filed form must use the table below $100,000. Qualifying surviving spouse / qualifying widow(er) (Form ND-1 filing status 5) uses the Married filing jointly column — the rate schedule is titled 'Married filing jointly and Qualifying widow(er)' and the footnote reads 'If a Qualifying widow(er), use the Married filing jointly column'; the engine's QSS-to-MFJ mapping is exactly correct. Printed '$X + Y% of excess over $Z' constants reconcile exactly with cumulative bracket sums (cent-rounded): Single $3,534.38 (exact 3,534.375), MFJ $3,906.83 (exact 3,906.825), MFS $1,953.41 (exact 1,953.4125), HoH $3,716.70 (exact); no divergence. No state standard deduction and no personal or dependent exemptions: ND starts from federal taxable income (Form 1040 line 15 -> ND-1 line 1b), which already reflects the FEDERAL standard or itemized deduction; nothing further is subtracted before the rates apply. ND additions and subtractions (ND-1 lines 2-17: e.g. net long-term capital gain exclusion of 40% (line 6), qualified dividend exclusion (line 13), Social Security benefit exclusion (line 15), U.S.-obligation interest (line 5)) are NOT modeled — if any apply, compute ND-1 line 18/19 on the form and supply that as the base. Marriage penalty credit (Form ND-1 line 22, maximum $287 for 2023) is a nonrefundable CREDIT subtracted from tax for joint filers, computed on the booklet worksheet — it is NOT an income exemption and is not modeled by this op. Full-year nonresidents and part-year residents do not use this computation directly: their tax comes from Schedule ND-1NR line 23 (the full-year tax prorated by the ND income ratio); this pack reproduces the full-year-resident tax on ND-1 line 20 only. Alternate computations not modeled: farm income averaging via Schedule ND-1FA and tax on proceeds from the sale of a research expense credit via Schedule ND-1CS — ND-1 line 20 directs those filers to the instructions. ND does NOT conform to federal income tax treaties (booklet p.5): treaty-exempt income is effectively rebuilt into the base via a Pro Forma 1040NR that disregards treaty provisions, whose line 15 becomes ND-1 line 1b.
